text: Virtually every public cloud VM image and container base image you'll touch in this field runs on Linux, not Windows. That's not a coincidence or a preference — it comes down to cost, distro design, and footprint, and this lesson walks through all three before we get into the shell itself.

The fastest way to confirm what a cloud VM is actually running is one command: cat /etc/os-release. On an Ubuntu box it reports a NAME field, a VERSION field, and an ID like ubuntu or debian. That single file, present on every modern distro, is the first thing worth checking whenever you're troubleshooting a server you didn't build yourself.

Three distro families matter most in cloud and DevOps work. Debian and Ubuntu use the apt package manager, and Ubuntu is the single most common default VM image you'll see offered across AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud. Red Hat Enterprise Linux, CentOS, and Fedora use yum or dnf instead, and that family dominates traditional enterprise data centers. Amazon Linux is AWS's own RHEL-derived distro, purpose-built to run well on EC2, and it's often the default AMI when you launch a new instance there.

Containers push the size question even further than virtual machines did. A minimal Linux base image like Alpine measures a few megabytes, and even a full Ubuntu container image stays under eighty. A Windows Server Core container image, by contrast, runs into multiple gigabytes. That gap is exactly why Docker Hub's official images, Kubernetes worker nodes, and serverless container platforms all assume a Linux userland underneath, even when the person building the image is sitting at a Windows laptop.

Put it together: no per-instance license fee, distro families purpose-built for servers and containers, and a footprint light enough to boot in milliseconds. That's the real reason Linux is the default operating system across every major cloud provider. Next up: the Linux filesystem hierarchy — where everything actually lives, and why that matters the first time something breaks.
